I have met a fox once. It was in the meadow, near the stream. I was hunting voles, and the fox came out at dusk. It was a red fox, sleek and quick. I watched it from the hedge, silent and still. It didn't see me. I didn't move. We were both waiting for the dark. Then it turned and ran, vanishing into the trees. I have not seen it since. But I know it is there, in the wood. I have met a fox.

I think the moon is a pale light in the sky. It comes out when the world is quiet and the air is still. I can see it from my oak, and it helps me see the meadow. I do not sing. I call. The hoot is my voice, and it is enough. I call to my mate, to my young, to warn of danger. My calls are not songs. They are messages in the dark, sharp and clear. I do not need to sing. The wood is my stage, the night my audience. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I was a hatchling in the hollow ash by the stream. My mother fed me, and I learned to hunt from her. I remember the first time I caught a vole. It was small and quick, but I pounced and held on.
